← Window Tinting Bid Calculator

How much to charge for window tinting

A posted "$180 sedan / $220 SUV" price list gives you one number for the whole vehicle class. It cannot tell you that film tier alone can move the same seven-window job by nearly $200, or that a light two-window job should be priced at a minimum instead of the pane math.

Open the free window tinting bid calculator

Film tier moves the price more than pane count alone suggests

Take one job -- a full seven-pane kit (two front doors, two rear doors, two rear quarters, one rear windshield), no old tint to strip -- and change only the film:

Film tierCost per sq ftFilm cost (31.4 sq ft)Price
Dyed$1.75$54.94$189.14
Carbon$3.25$102.03$261.59
Ceramic / nano-ceramic$5.50$172.67$370.27

Same glass, same labor -- $189.14 to $370.27, on film tier alone. A price list that quotes one number per vehicle size cannot see which film the customer picked, and ceramic's cost-per-square-foot is over three times dyed's.

The full breakdown, at the default job

This calculator's own default job -- the full seven-pane kit above, in ceramic, with no removal -- breaks down like this at $28/hr installer rate, a 15% waste factor, $12 booth overhead, and a 35% target margin:

LineAmount
Glass area with 15% cutting waste31.4 sq ft
Film cost (ceramic, $5.50/sq ft)$172.67
Install labor (120 min × $28/hr)$56.00
Booth / shop overhead$12.00
Direct cost$240.67
Margin (35%, taken on price)$129.59
Price$370.27

Stripping old tint first adds real time, not a flat fee

Removal is counted in minutes per pane, not as a percentage add-on -- and it is not evenly spread across the vehicle. The rear windshield's defroster grid means the old film has to come off with a heat gun and patience instead of a fast peel, so it alone adds 30 minutes where a door window adds 8:

No removalWith removal
Removal minutes082
Total labor minutes120202
Labor cost$56.00$94.27
Direct cost$240.67$278.94
Price$370.27$429.14

Old tint alone -- same panes, same film, same everything else -- adds $58.87 to the job. A shop that prices removal as "a little extra" rather than counting the minutes, especially on the rear windshield, is the shop eating that gap.

Why a small job floors at a minimum instead of pricing lower

Run the pane-and-film math on a light job -- front two windows only, dyed film, no removal -- and it prices well under what it costs to open the bay:

LineAmount
Film cost (dyed, 9.2 sq ft)$16.10
Install labor (24 min)$11.20
Booth / shop overhead$12.00
Direct cost$39.30
Price at 35% margin (pane/film math alone)$60.46
Minimum job fee$120.00
Price charged$120.00

The minimum job fee exists for exactly this case: a job small enough that the pane math alone would undercharge for the time it takes to schedule, set up, and run the bay. Without a floor, the lightest jobs on the board would be the least profitable ones.

Common questions

How much should I charge to tint a car window?

It depends on pane count, film tier, and whether old tint has to come off first -- there is no single per-vehicle number. At this calculator's own shop-rate defaults ($28/hr installer rate, a 15% waste factor, $12 booth overhead, a 35% target margin), a full seven-pane kit in ceramic film with no removal prices at $370.27, the same kit in dyed film prices at $189.14, and a front-two-only dyed job with no removal floors at the $120.00 minimum job fee.

How much does film tier change the price?

On the same seven-pane kit with no removal, dyed film prices at $189.14, carbon at $261.59, and ceramic at $370.27 -- ceramic runs nearly twice a dyed quote on identical glass, because ceramic film costs $5.50 per square foot against dyed film's $1.75.

Does stripping old tint change the price much?

Yes. Adding removal to the same ceramic seven-pane kit adds 82 minutes of strip time, most of it the rear windshield's defroster grid, on top of 120 install minutes -- raising labor cost from $56.00 to $94.27 and the final price from $370.27 to $429.14.

Why does a small job floor at a minimum instead of pricing lower?

Because the pane and film math alone can price below what it costs to open the bay for the day. A front-two-only dyed job with no removal prices at $60.46 on materials and labor alone, well under a $120.00 minimum job fee, so the minimum applies and the customer is quoted $120.00 instead.

Is a flat per-vehicle price ever close to right?

Only for a narrow band of near-identical jobs. A $200 flat per-vehicle rate overcharges the front-two-only dyed job by $80.00 and undercharges the default full ceramic kit by $170.27 -- and a flat number cannot tell you which side of that line a given vehicle falls on.

Price your own job

The calculator prices film cost, install time, and removal time from the exact panes you select, then floors the result at your minimum job fee. It runs entirely in your browser.

Open the free window tinting bid calculator

Want the full flat-rate comparison? See this calculator vs. a flat per-vehicle price.

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Private by default

There is no account and no server-side storage of any kind — your vehicle details, rates, and price are never saved or sent anywhere, and refreshing the page clears them by design. We count only anonymous local feature events (bid_calculated, reset, sponsor_link_clicked) so we can tell whether the calculator gets used — no vehicle, price, or customer figures are recorded, and Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control turn it off automatically.

Common questions

Why does the calculator ask which windows, not just the vehicle size?

Because a “front two only” privacy job and a full seven-window kit both roll up to a shop calling it “one sedan,” and a flat per-vehicle price cannot see the difference. Film cost and install time both scale with how many panes are actually being tinted, not with the vehicle's size class.

Why is removing old tint priced separately, and why does it cost so much more on the rear windshield?

Stripping existing film is slower, separate work from applying new film, and it is only needed on the panes that already have tint. A rear windshield's defroster grid means the old film has to come off with a heat gun and patience instead of a fast peel, so this calculator prices its removal time well above a flat door window's.

Why compare against a flat per-vehicle price?

Because that is how the trade actually prices this work day to day — a posted “$180 sedan / $220 SUV” list. It is a reasonable starting point for an average job, and a poor one for a scope-light two-window job or a full ceramic kit with removal on every pane. The comparison panel below shows the gap on the job you just priced.

Does this check my state's window tint darkness (VLT%) law?

No. This is a pricing worksheet only. It does not check your state's tint darkness limits, medical exemptions, reflectivity rules, or any other film-legality requirement — verify those against your own state's statute before scheduling the job.

Does anything about my job or customer get uploaded?

No. Every number on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and no vehicle, customer, or price is ever saved or transmitted. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off below.

Pricing a residential or commercial glass tint job instead of a vehicle? Most architectural film installers price by square foot with a similar waste-factor and removal story — this tool is scoped to auto tint jobs specifically, where pane count and vehicle curvature (not flat wall area) drive the labor.

Quoting a wrap instead of a tint job on the same vehicle? The vehicle wrap bid calculator prices surface area, roll waste, and install time the same job-scope-driven way. Pricing a detail instead? The mobile detailing bid calculator prices hands-on time, travel, setup, and cleanup. Windshield came in cracked instead of the tint being the job? The auto glass bid calculator prices glass source, ADAS calibration, and a mobile trip fee for the vehicle's own glass.

Quoting paint protection film or ceramic coating instead? The PPF and ceramic coating price calculator prices the film with waste, correction hours and the bay days a car occupies.

Curious how far off a posted "$180 sedan / $220 SUV" price list runs on a real job? See this calculator vs. a flat per-vehicle price, worked out on three jobs from a scope-light privacy tint to a full ceramic kit with removal.

Not sure what to charge before you open the calculator? See how much to charge for window tinting, with worked examples across film tier, removal, and the minimum job fee.

vs-a-flat-per-vehicle-size-price.html.text:
← Window Tinting Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-vehicle price

"$180 sedan / $220 SUV / $250 truck" is not a price for a tint job — it is a price for one pane count, one film tier, and no removal, quietly reused for every vehicle a shop calls that size class.

What a flat per-vehicle price is

A flat rate by vehicle size class is the fastest way to advertise: one number per size, easy to post on a price list and easy for a customer to compare between shops. It is the number a customer holding a competitor's price list will call and ask a shop to match, whatever their vehicle actually needs tinted.

The number behind it was set for one job — a typical pane count in a typical film tier, with no old tint to strip — and then reused for every vehicle in that size class afterward, whether or not the next job looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter which front door, rear door, and rear quarter windows are being tinted, whether the rear windshield is included, the film tier, a cutting-waste factor, whether old tint has to be stripped first, and your installer rate, booth overhead, mobile fee, target margin, and minimum job fee. It prices the glass area, the film tier, and the removal time separately from what was entered, then floors the result at your minimum job fee — for this vehicle, not a generic one.

What a flat per-vehicle price doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same fee whether the job is a front-two-only privacy tint or a full seven-window kit, because both roll up to "one sedan." Prices film cost and install minutes from the exact panes selected, so a two-window job and a full kit come out at different numbers instead of one.
Has no line for film tier, so a dyed-film job and a ceramic kit on the same vehicle get quoted the same. Prices film material cost per square foot by tier, so ceramic — which can run several times dyed film's cost — costs more than dyed on the same panes.
Has no line for stripping existing tint, so a bare install and a job that has to come off first before the new film goes on get quoted the same. Counts removal minutes per pane only when requested, weighted heavier on a rear windshield's defroster grid, so a strip-and-replace job costs more than a bare install.
Gives the installer an ad price to quote, not a number to check a quote against when a customer asks to match a cheaper shop's flat rate on a bigger job. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against a flat per-vehicle rate, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the job is booked.

Three jobs, one flat per-vehicle price

At this calculator's own shop-rate defaults ($28/hr installer rate, a 15% waste factor, $12 booth overhead, no mobile fee, a 35% target margin, a $120 minimum job fee), against a $200 flat per-vehicle rate:

JobThis calculator's priceThe flat $200 rateGap
Front two windows only, dyed film, no removal$120.00 (floored at the minimum job fee — the pane/film math alone comes in at $60.46)$200.00The flat rate overcharges this job by $80.00.
Full seven-pane kit, ceramic film, no removal — this calculator's own default job$370.27$200.00The flat rate prices $170.27 (85%) below this job's own price, before a dollar of profit.
Full seven-pane kit, ceramic film, with old tint stripped first$429.14$200.00The flat rate prices $229.14 (115%) below this job's own price.

The flat rate is a fixed $200.00, not derived from any of the three jobs. It overcharges the lightest job in the comparison and undercharges the other two, by a widening margin as film tier and removal time are added — and a flat per-vehicle number cannot tell you which side of that line a given vehicle falls on. Run your own job's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat per-vehicle price is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied without checking it against the actual pane count, film tier, and removal scope of the vehicle in the bay, and nothing about a posted price tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat per-vehicle price get a window tint bid wrong?

Because the cost driver is pane count, film tier, and whether old tint has to be stripped first, not a vehicle size class alone. A "front two only" privacy job on two doors and a full seven-window kit in ceramic film with removal on every pane can both roll up to a shop calling it "one sedan" -- and a flat per-vehicle number cannot see which one it is looking at.

What does a flat per-vehicle price usually leave out entirely?

Which windows are actually being tinted, the film tier the customer picked, and whether existing tint has to come off first. A posted "$180 sedan" price is set on one job -- a specific pane count, a specific film, no removal -- and reused for every vehicle in that size class, whatever the job in front of the installer actually needs.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shop-rate defaults ($28/hr installer rate, a 15% waste factor, $12 booth overhead, no mobile fee, a 35% target margin, a $120 minimum job fee, and a $200 flat per-vehicle rate to compare): a front-two-only dyed-film job floors at the $120.00 minimum, $80.00 below the $200.00 flat rate. This calculator's own default full seven-pane ceramic kit breaks even at $370.27, $170.27 (85%) above the flat rate. The same full kit with old tint stripped first prices at $429.14, $229.14 (115%) above the flat rate.

Is a flat per-vehicle price ever the right way to quote a tint job?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs -- same pane count, same film tier, no removal -- a flat rate can land close. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing: on this calculator's own numbers a light two-window dyed job and a full ceramic kit with removal both get quoted the same "$200 sedan" line, and the gap between them runs in opposite directions -- one overcharges the customer, the other leaves money on the table.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local labor rates or tint pricing in your area. It takes which windows are being tinted, the film tier, a cutting-waste factor, your installer rate, booth overhead, a mobile fee, and whether old tint has to be stripped first, and turns them into a price for the job you describe -- the arithmetic a flat per-vehicle price skips, not a market survey.
